presenceLabel: Illinois (Illiniwek) town or declared claim in this area
presenceNote: The story is an event of 1778 (two town points, no boundary). The only sourced boundary is the claim the Kaskaskia declared on 13 Aug 1803: two river reaches can be drawn; the inland calls follow unlocated ridges and are not drawn, so no area is closed. No Kentucky territory is shown. The page spans 1778–1803 to include the 1803 claim.
overlapNote: Piankashaw (Wabash side: the 1804 treaty Art. 2 acknowledges the Kaskaskia right to sell their ceded country, separated from Piankashaw land by the Wabash/Saline Creek and Wabash/Mississippi-tributary divides), Kickapoo (took part of Illinois 'by conquest from the Illinois nation', 1819 treaty), Potawatomi and Miami to the north and east. Shawnee and Cherokee Kentucky claims do not overlap (west bank of the claim is the Ohio).
basis: Kaskaskia treaty 1803 (text), Piankeshaw treaty 1804 Art. 2, NPS Clark NHP page, Wikipedia coordinates for the towns.

eras.label: July–Sept 1778 · Clark at Cahokia and Kaskaskia
eras.text: Clark took Kaskaskia, Prairie du Rocher and Cahokia in July 1778, then held a council at Cahokia in late summer with leaders of nearby tribes; many accepted the white belt of peace, many others stayed allied with the British (NPS). The two towns are approximate points, and the tint is an approximate general area of the Illinois towns on the Mississippi bottom, built from whole counties.

eras.label: 1803 · The claim the Kaskaskia declared
eras.text: By 1803 the Illinois tribes (Kaskaskia, Michigamea, Cahokia, Tamaroa) were 'reduced to a very small number' and consolidated as the Kaskaskia. On 13 Aug 1803 at Vincennes they ceded their Illinois lands, reserving about 350 acres at Kaskaskia, and declared their claim: up the Ohio from the Mississippi to Saline Creek, then along watershed ridges to the Illinois River basin and the Illinois mouth, and down the Mississippi. The tint is a general area of that claim built from whole counties; the ridge calls are not located, so its inland edge is a rough guess, not a boundary.

General area of the claim the Kaskaskia declared on 13 Aug 1803: from the Mississippi up the Ohio to Saline Creek, then along ridges toward the Illinois River basin. The Ohio and Mississippi reaches are sourced; the inland calls follow unlocated ridges, so the tint is built from whole southern and south-central Illinois counties and is only a general area. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.
